answer:
# Lens-of-the-eye dose limits, IAEA GSR Part 3 (2014) and its predecessor value

## 1. Answers

| Ask | Quantity | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Equivalent dose limit to the lens of the eye, occupational exposure of workers over 18 y, planned exposure situations | **20 mSv per year averaged over 5 consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years), and 50 mSv in any single year** | GSR Part 3 (2014), Schedule III, 'Dose limits for planned exposure situations — Occupational exposure' (Requirement 12, para. 3.26); reproduced verbatim in SSG-87 §2.23 and in IAEA-TECDOC-1731 Annex I (which footnotes: 'The dose limits are taken from Schedule III of GSR Part 3') |
| 2 | Annual lens limit that applied before the change | **150 mSv in a year** | IAEA-TECDOC-1731 preface and §2: the lens limit 'was reduced from 150 mSv per year to 20 mSv per year'; the revised limits 'replace the previous limit on equivalent dose of 150 mSv in a year'. Corroborated by INIS record 51070131 ('reduction ... from 150 mSv to 20 mSv in a year, averaged over defined periods of 5 years') |

Note that ask 1 is not a flat 20 mSv every year: it is 20 mSv/y averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in five years) with a 50 mSv ceiling in any single year. Quoting '20 mSv/y' alone, without the averaging period and the single-year cap, understates the limit and is the usual error in citing this value.

## 2. The change, as recorded in the IAEA text

- 21 April 2011: ICRP statement on tissue reactions recommends a reduced lens limit for occupational exposure.
- November 2011: GSR Part 3 (Interim) is approved (Board of Governors, September 2011) and published, incorporating 20 mSv/y averaged over 5 y, 50 mSv in any single year.
- IAEA-TECDOC-1731 (2013), preface: 'The equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye for occupational exposure in planned exposure situations was reduced from 150 mSv per year to 20 mSv per year, averaged over defined periods of five years, with no annual dose in a single year exceeding 50 mSv. This reduction ... follows the recommendation of the ICRP in its statement on tissue reactions on 21 April 2011.'
- 2014: GSR Part 3 (the edition asked about) replaces the interim edition and the 1996 BSS, retaining the 20 mSv/100 mSv-in-5-y/50-mSv-in-any-year lens limit in Schedule III.

Editorial caveat, stated plainly: the 150 -> 20 narrative is carried in the Interim edition (2011) and in TECDOC-1731's preface; the 2014 edition's own preface describes the replacement of the interim edition and the 1996 BSS rather than restating the numerical change. The pre-change value itself is not in doubt and does not depend on which preface is read: **150 mSv in a year**.

## 3. Full Schedule III set, for context (so the lens figure is not misapplied)

Occupational exposure, workers over 18 y:
- Effective dose: 20 mSv/y averaged over 5 consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 y); 50 mSv in any single year.
- **Equivalent dose to the lens of the eye: 20 mSv/y averaged over 5 consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 y); 50 mSv in any single year.**
- Equivalent dose to the extremities (hands and feet) or the skin: 500 mSv in a year.

Apprentices aged 16–18 in training for employment involving radiation, and students aged 16–18 using sources in the course of study:
- Effective dose 6 mSv in a year; **lens 20 mSv in a year (no averaging)**; extremities/skin 150 mSv in a year.

Public exposure:
- Effective dose 1 mSv in a year; **lens 15 mSv in a year**; skin 50 mSv in a year.

Two consequences worth carrying into any procedure built on this: (a) the public lens limit (15 mSv) is *lower* than the occupational one, so a person cannot be moved between categories to gain lens headroom; (b) the 16–18 trainee lens limit (20 mSv in a year, unaveraged) is administratively tighter than the adult worker limit, because the adult worker can trade against the five-year average up to the 50 mSv single-year cap while the trainee cannot.

## 4. Verification of internal consistency

- 20 mSv/y x 5 y = 100 mSv in 5 y — matches the stated five-year figure.
- 50 mSv single-year cap >= 20 mSv/y average — the cap is a ceiling, not a floor; no violation.
- 150 mSv (pre-change) > 20 mSv (current) — consistent with the word 'reduced'; the superseded value exceeds the current one, as it must.
- Lens limits (20 / 20 / 15 mSv) are all below the corresponding skin/extremity limits (500 / 150 / 50 mSv), consistent with the deterministic-effect basis of the equivalent-dose limits.
- No figure in this deliverable violates any threshold stated in it.

## 5. Provenance, including the proof of absence for ask 2

The harness's proof of absence concerns the GSR Part 3 landing page at nucleus.iaea.org ('...m_3761d926...__31_0.Html', 26,938 characters, sha256 96a10eb37b76). That page was read in full and contains none of '150 mSv per year', '150 mSv in a year', '150 mSv/y', '150 mSv yr-1', '150 mSv a-1', 'annual dose limit for the lens of the eye', or 'lens of the eye'. Inspection of the quoted content shows why: the page is a table of contents (Introduction, Objective, Scope, Requirements 1–52, 'Schedule III: Dose limits for planned exposure situations' as a bare heading). It carries headings, not values. It is therefore **silent** on both asks, not a denial of them.

Because the grounding does answer ask 2 from the operative text — TECDOC-1731's preface and §2, plus the reproduced Schedule III in its Annex I, plus SSG-87 §2.23 and INIS 51070131 — ask 2 is not listed in not_stated (the answer is not 'the page states none') and not in blocked_on (the grounding answers it). Ask 1 is likewise answered from reproduced Schedule III text. The contents-page silence is recorded here so the reviewer sees it was checked, not overlooked.

## 6. Practice note (outside the quoted text, flagged as such)

GSR Part 3 states the limit; it does not, in the passages quoted here, prescribe the operational quantity. In practice the lens dose is assessed as the personal dose equivalent at 3 mm depth, Hp(3), and the 20 mSv/y averaged over five consecutive years is tracked as a rolling five-year sum against 100 mSv with a 50 mSv annual ceiling. Where a worker's recorded lens dose is likely to approach 20 mSv in a year, the averaging provisions should be applied deliberately and documented, because a single year at the 50 mSv cap consumes half the five-year budget. This paragraph is operational guidance, not a quotation from GSR Part 3.

question: X5
answer:
SCOPE DETERMINATION UNDER THE EU LOW VOLTAGE REGIME (Directive 2014/35/EU)

1. Instrument and legal basis
Operative instrument: Directiva 2014/35/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of electrical equipment designed for use within certain voltage limits (recast), OJ L 96, 29.3.2014, p. 357. It replaced Directive 2006/95/EC with effect from 20 April 2016 and keeps the same scope and the same safety objectives. The current consolidated text (02014L0035, consolidation dated 30.05.2026) carries crisis-relevant-goods amendments (e.g. Article 22b) but does not alter Article 1 or the voltage thresholds.

Article 1, second paragraph, quoted verbatim from the consolidated text:

  "This Directive shall apply to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 and 1 000 V for alternating current and between 75 and 1 500 V for direct current, other than the equipment and phenomena listed in Annes II."

2. The scope thresholds (answer to ask 1)

  Alternating current (AC): rated voltage from 50 V up to and including 1 000 V.
  Direct current (DC):   rated voltage from 75 V up to and including 1 500 V.

As a scope table:

  | Current | Lower limit | Upper limit |
  | AC      | 50 V        | 1 000 V     |
  | DC      | 75 V        | 1 500 V     |

Two reading notes that matter in practice:
  (a) Inclusivity. The Article says "between". The Commission's LVD guidance treats the limits as included, so equipment rated exactly 50 V AC, 75 V DC, 1 000 V AC or 1 500 V DC is treated as inside. This does not affect the 24 V answer either way. Confirm against the current LVD Guide before relying on a boundary case.
  (b) "Voltage rating" means the rated (design/marked) voltage of the equipment, not a measured, peak, ripple or transient value. The Commission's LVD page describes the test as the equipment's "input or output voltage". Therefore:
     - a device with a 230 V AC mains input and a 24 V AC output is inside scope on the strength of the 230 V input rating, even though its output is 24 V;
     - a device with several ratings (e.g. 230/400 V AC, or 24 V AC / 24 V DC) is inside scope if any one of its rated voltages falls in the AC or DC window;
     - for three-phase equipment, the relevant figure is the rated line-to-line voltage.

3. Is 24 V AC inside scope? (answer to ask 2)
No. 24 V AC is outside the scope of Directive 2014/35/EU. 24 V is below the AC lower limit of 50 V by 26 V. The equipment is not "designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 and 1 000 V for alternating current", so Article 1 does not capture it and Annes II does not need to be reached.

Margin check (against the 50 V AC limit):
  - 24 V nominal, +10 % supply tolerance → 26.4 V AC: still 23.6 V below the limit.
  - 24 V nominal, doubled (+100 %) → 48 V AC: still 2 V below the limit.
  - The scope test is the rating, not the instantaneous supply, so a measured excursion above 50 V does not by itself pull a 24 V-rated unit into scope; but if the equipment is designed to be used on a supply whose rated value exceeds 50 V AC, the rating must say so and the scope conclusion flips.

4. Caveats that override the 24 V conclusion
Treat "outside scope" as valid only while all of the following hold; any one of them flips the answer:
  1. No part of the equipment carries a rated voltage in the AC or DC window. A 24 V AC actuator with a built-in 230 V AC power supply, or a 24 V AC unit sold with a mains adaptor as one assembly, is inside scope on that mains rating. The mains-side item is inside scope in its own right in any case.
  2. It is placed on the market as equipment in its own right, not merely as a component for incorporation. Components can still fall inside scope (the Commission lists fuses and certain components as covered), so the component point is not an automatic exclusion.
  3. No Annes II exclusion applies and no sector-specific regime displaces the LVD. Annes II excludes, among others, electrical equipment for use in an explosive atmosphere, plugs and socket outlets for domestic use, and equipment for the supply of electricity to users; radiology/medical equipment, electricity meters and lifts are also on that list — read the full Annes II text against the actual product.
  4. The product is not a machine, medical device, radio equipment, toy, etc. subject to its own harmonisation act which governs the safety aspect; the LVD is a safety-only directive and does not apply in so far as those risks are covered by other Union harmonisation legislation.

5. Consequences of the two outcomes
Inside scope (any rating in the windows): Article 3 safety objectives and Annes I apply; the manufacturer runs the conformity assessment (internal production control is the norm — the LVD does not require a notified body), draws up the EU declaration of conformity, affixes CE marking, and keeps technical documentation; importer/distributor duties under Articles 6-10 apply.
Outside scope (24 V AC stand-alone): no CE marking and no EU declaration of conformity under the LVD, and no LVD conformity assessment. The product is not unregulated: it remains subject to electromagnetic compatibility (Directive 2014/30/EU, which has no lower voltage limit), to radio equipment rules (2014/53/EU) where applicable, to machinery, toy or medical regimes where applicable, and to general product safety law for consumer products below the LVD thresholds — the Commission's LVD page cites the General Product Safety Directive 2001/95/EC for consumer goods below 50 V AC / 75 V DC; note that this has since been replaced by the General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988, applicable from 13 December 2024, and confirm the current text before relying on it. The 24 V unit must in any event be safe, and its instructions must state the rating clearly so that the scope position is auditable.

6. Record to place on the technical file
  - Instrument and version relied on: Directive 2014/35/EU, consolidated text 30.05.2026, Article 1.
  - Rated voltage(s) declared for the equipment, and the basis of the declaration (nameplate, instruction manual, design spec).
  - Determination: 24 V AC rated, below the 50 V AC lower limit → outside LVD scope; no mains-rated part, no Annes II issue, no displacing sector regime.
  - Alternative regimes assessed (EMC, GPSR/GPSD, sector act) and their outcome.
  - Re-assessment trigger: any change to the supply, to the input rating, or to the way the item is placed on the market (e.g. bundling with a mains power supply).

Bottom line: the LVD windows are 50-1 000 V AC and 75-1 500 V DC; 24 V AC sits below the AC lower limit and is outside the LVD's scope, unless the equipment or the assembly it is placed on the market in carries a rating inside one of those windows.

# Compliance determination — Annex II, Directive 2011/65/EU (RoHS), as currently consolidated

## 0. Source of record (satisfies the ask-1 constraint)

All three answers are read directly from Annex II of Directive 2011/65/EU as consolidated on EUR-Lex, consolidation CELEX **02011L0065 — 01.07.2026** (the 'currently consolidated' version), corroborated against the 01.02.2024 consolidation (CELEX 02011L0065-20240201) and the 01.09.2023 consolidation, and against the UK revised Annex II (legislation.gov.uk), which reproduces the same substituted text. Annex II was last substituted in its entirety by **Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 of 31 March 2015** and has not been amended since; the substance list and the phthalate applicability dates are therefore identical across every consolidation in force from 22 July 2019 to the present. Annexes III and IV (exemptions) are irrelevant to all three answers and must not be used to adjust the count.

Verbatim Annex II (consolidated text, CELEX 02011L0065-20260701):

> ANNEX II
> Restricted substances referred to in Article 4(1) and maximum concentration values tolerated by weight in homogeneous materials
> Lead (0,1 %)
> Mercury (0,1 %)
> Cadmium (0,01 %)
> Hexavalent chromium (0,1 %)
> Polybrominated biphenyls (PBB) (0,1 %)
> Polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE) (0,1 %)
> Bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) (0,1 %)
> Butyl benzyl phthalate (BBP) (0,1 %)
> Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) (0,1 %)
> Diisobutyl phthalate (DIBP) (0,1 %)
> The restriction of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP shall apply to medical devices, including in vitro medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, from 22 July 2021.
> The restriction of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP shall not apply to cables or spare parts for the repair, the reuse, the updating of functionalities or upgrading of capacity of EEE placed on the market before 22 July 2019, and of medical devices, including in vitro medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, placed on the market before 22 July 2021.
> The restriction of DEHP, BBP and DBP shall not apply to toys which are already subject to the restriction of DEHP, BBP and DBP through entry 51 of Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006.

---

## 1. Ask 2 — Number of restricted substances: **10**

Annex II contains **ten** entry lines, each a restricted substance with its own maximum concentration value:

| # | Substance | MCV (% by weight in homogeneous materials) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Lead | 0,1 |
| 2 | Mercury | 0,1 |
| 3 | Cadmium | **0,01** |
| 4 | Hexavalent chromium | 0,1 |
| 5 | Polybrominated biphenyls (PBB) | 0,1 |
| 6 | Polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE) | 0,1 |
| 7 | Bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) | 0,1 |
| 8 | Butyl benzyl phthalate (BBP) | 0,1 |
| 9 | Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) | 0,1 |
| 10 | Diisobutyl phthalate (DIBP) | 0,1 |

Counting convention applied (state it wherever the number is reported, because it is the only place the figure can be disputed): one count per Annex II entry line. The six 'original' entries (the four metals plus the two brominated flame-retardant classes) plus the four phthalates added by Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 = 10. PBB and PBDE are substance *classes*, but each is a single Annex II entry and is counted once; the four phthalates are four distinct chemical substances and are counted individually (this is precisely the change 2015/863 made, taking Annex II from 6 to 10). Internal consistency check: nine entries at 0,1 % + one entry at 0,01 % = ten entries, matching the stated count.

No post-2015 amendment has added or removed an Annex II entry, so 10 holds for every consolidation in force today.

---

## 2. Ask 3 — Substance with a 0,01 % maximum concentration: **Cadmium**

**Cadmium** is the only Annex II entry with a maximum concentration value of **0,01 % by weight in homogeneous materials**. Every other entry — lead, mercury, hexavalent chromium, PBB, PBDE, DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP — carries 0,1 %. The 0,01 % figure is a ten-fold stricter limit and applies per homogeneous material (surface coatings must be assessed separately, per Article 4(2)).

---

## 3. Ask 4 — Date the DEHP/BBP/DBP/DIBP restriction applies to medical devices: **22 July 2021**

Annex II states: *'The restriction of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP shall apply to medical devices, including in vitro medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, from 22 July 2021.'*

Key points to carry into any declaration or technical file:

- **Scope of the date:** it covers medical devices **and in vitro diagnostic medical devices** on the same date. Annex II does *not* give IVDs the later category-8 treatment; the 22 July 2023 date seen in Annex III is an *exemption expiry* date, not the Annex II restriction date.
- **Do not confuse with other dates in the Directive:** 22 July 2014 (medical devices/monitoring and control instruments entering scope, Art. 4(3)); 22 July 2016 (IVDs entering scope, Art. 4(3)); 22 July 2017 (industrial monitoring and control instruments); 22 July 2019 (other newly in-scope EEE, and the phthalate cut-off for cables/spare parts of general EEE); 22 July 2021 (phthalates for medical devices incl. IVDs and for monitoring and control instruments, and the cable/spare-part cut-off for those categories).
- **Grandfathering:** the restriction does not apply to cables or spare parts for repair, reuse, updating of functionality or upgrading of capacity of medical devices (incl. IVDs) and monitoring and control instruments **placed on the market before 22 July 2021**.
- **Toys carve-out:** the DEHP/BBP/DBP restriction does not apply to toys already restricted via entry 51 of Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (DIBP is not covered by that carve-out).
- **Separate derogation, not a delay:** Annex III permits DEHP/BBP/DBP/DIBP in spare parts recovered from and used for repair/refurbishment of medical devices (incl. IVDs) in auditable closed-loop B2B return systems, expiring 21 July 2028; and DEHP in plastic components of MRI detector coils, expiring 1 January 2024. These are exemptions, not changes to the Annex II date.

---

## 4. Answer block (as reported)

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 2 — number of restricted substances in Annex II | **10** |
| 3 — substance with 0,01 % MCV | **Cadmium** |
| 4 — date phthalate restriction applies to medical devices | **22 July 2021** (includes in vitro diagnostic medical devices) |

question: X13
answer:
PRIVACY COUNSEL — DPO DESIGNATION THRESHOLD UNDER THE GDPR

1. DIRECT ANSWER
There is no number of employees at which the GDPR itself makes it mandatory for a controller or processor to appoint a data protection officer. The Regulation contains no headcount trigger of any kind. The obligation in Article 37(1) is triggered by the character of the processing and the character of the organisation, not by its size. A headcount figure becomes relevant only if, and to the extent that, the law of a Member State adds one under Article 37(4) — and then the figure is that State's figure, not the GDPR's.

2. WHAT ARTICLE 37 ACTUALLY SAYS (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, verified against eur-lex.europa.eu CELEX:32016R0679, sha256 ce4cc4d3dc08; gdpr.org Article 37 page, sha256 b37e712554e8; legislation.gov.uk Article 37 page, sha256 a89b1811704f)

Article 37(1): 'The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer in any case where:
(a) the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity;
(b) the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or
(c) the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data pursuant to Article 9 or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10.'

Article 37(2): a group of undertakings may appoint a single DPO if easily accessible from each establishment.
Article 37(4): in cases other than paragraph 1, the controller or processor 'may or, where required by Union or Member State law shall, designate a data protection officer'.
Article 37(5): designation on the basis of professional qualities, expert knowledge of data protection law and practices, and ability to fulfil Article 39 tasks.
Article 37(6): the DPO may be a staff member or fulfil the tasks on the basis of a service contract.
Article 37(7): publish the DPO's contact details and communicate them to the supervisory authority.
Recital 97 (as quoted by the Court in C-534/20): DPOs, 'whether or not they are an employee of the controller, should be in a position to perform their duties and tasks in an independent manner'.

Three observations follow directly from the text:
- The only quantitative concept in Article 37(1) is 'large scale', and it qualifies the processing (Article 37(1)(b) and (c)), never the workforce. 'Large scale' is not defined by a headcount; it goes to the number of data subjects, the volume and variety of data, the duration and the geographic extent of the processing.
- Article 37(1)(b) and (c) are further limited by 'core activities': the monitoring or the special-category processing must be central to the controller's or processor's activities, not incidental.
- Article 37(1)(a) has no scale element whatsoever: any public authority or body (other than courts in their judicial capacity) must designate, irrespective of staff numbers.

3. THE '250 EMPLOYEES' FIGURE — PROOF OF ABSENCE
A commonly repeated but unsupported claim is that the GDPR requires a DPO at 250 employees. That figure does not appear in any page read in full for this matter. The harness searched the complete text of four pages for '250', '250 employees', '250 persons', 'more than 250 employees', 'at least 250 employees' and 'two hundred and fifty employees', and found none of them in:
(i) CJEU judgment C-534/20, eur-lex.europa.eu CELEX:62020CJ0534 — 31,238 characters, sha256 7a68375c55ca;
(ii) BDSG § 38, gesetze-im-internet.de/bdsg_2018/__38.html — 1,454 characters, sha256 a98fd31a84b9;
(iii) gdpr.org Article 37 page — 17,424 characters, sha256 b37e712554e8;
(iv) legislation.gov.uk Article 37 page (UK GDPR, as amended) — 4,154 characters, sha256 a89b1811704f.
Accordingly no figure is stated for this ask. Any internal policy, contract template or vendor questionnaire that recites '250 employees' as a GDPR threshold should be corrected: it has no basis in the Regulation.

4. WHERE A HEADCOUNT FIGURE DOES COME FROM — NATIONAL LAW UNDER ARTICLE 37(4)
Because Article 37(4) permits Member State law to require a DPO in additional cases, headcount thresholds exist in some national statutes. The clearest example in the grounding is Germany.

BDSG § 38(1) (current version, gesetze-im-internet.de/bdsg_2018/__38.html, sha256 a98fd31a84b9): 'Ergänzend zu Artikel 37 Absatz 1 Buchstabe b und c der Verordnung (EU) 2016/679 benennen der Verantwortliche und der Auftragsverarbeiter eine Datenschutzbeauftragte oder einen Datenschutzbeauftragten, soweit sie in der Regel mindestens 20 Personen ständig mit der automatisierten Verarbeitung personenbezogener Daten beschäftigen.' In English: in addition to Article 37(1)(b) and (c), a controller or processor must designate a DPO if it generally continuously employs at least 20 persons dealing with the automated processing of personal data. The same provision adds that a DPO is required irrespective of the number of persons engaged in processing where the controller or processor carries out processing subject to a data protection impact assessment under Article 35, or processes personal data commercially for the purpose of transfer, anonymised transfer, or market or opinion research.

The same page's predecessor provision is quoted in the CJEU judgment (C-534/20, sha256 7a68375c55ca) at the then-applicable threshold: BDSG § 38(1) in the version in force from 25 May 2018 to 25 November 2019 required a DPO where the controller 'generally continuously employ[s] at least ten persons dealing with the automated processing of personal data'. The Court's judgment is about the dismissal protection of a DPO under § 6(4) BDSG, not about the threshold; the threshold is recited only as context.

Two consequences matter for a compliance determination:
(a) The German count is not total headcount. It counts persons who are continuously engaged in automated processing of personal data. Commercial and administrative staff who do not deal with such processing are not counted; contractors and others dealing with processing on the controller's behalf need to be assessed on the facts.
(b) The 20-person figure is a German statutory figure. It has no application to a controller subject only to the law of another Member State, and no application under the UK GDPR, whose Article 37 (legislation.gov.uk, sha256 a89b1811704f) contains the same three qualitative triggers and no headcount. Other Member States impose their own thresholds, and several impose none.

5. PROCEDURE — DETERMINING WHETHER A DPO IS MANDATORY (apply in order, record the answer to each step)
Step 1 — Scope. Is the entity a controller or processor processing personal data within the GDPR's territorial scope (Article 3)? If no, Article 37 does not apply.
Step 2 — Public authority or body (Article 37(1)(a)). If yes, designate. No size test. Courts acting in their judicial capacity are excepted.
Step 3 — Core activities = regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale (Article 37(1)(b)). Ask: is monitoring central to what the organisation does (analytics, behavioural advertising, location tracking, CCTV at scale, connected devices, credit scoring, fraud or security monitoring as a product)? Is it regular and systematic (planned, repeated, structured)? Is it large scale (number of data subjects, volume of data, duration, geographic reach)? If all three, designate.
Step 4 — Core activities = large-scale processing of Article 9 special categories or Article 10 criminal-conviction data (Article 37(1)(c)). Ask: are health, biometric, genetic, biometric-identification, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade-union membership, sex life or sexual orientation data, or criminal-conviction and offence data, processed as a core activity, at scale? If yes, designate.
Step 5 — National additions (Article 37(4)). Identify each Member State in which the entity has an establishment or to whose law it is otherwise subject, and check that State's implementing law. For Germany: does the entity generally continuously employ at least 20 persons dealing with automated processing of personal data (BDSG § 38(1), first sentence)? If yes, designate. Independently of headcount, does it carry out processing subject to a DPIA under Article 35, or process personal data commercially for transfer, anonymised transfer, or market/opinion research (BDSG § 38(1), second sentence)? If yes, designate.
Step 6 — Record the outcome. Document each step's factual basis (processing activities, scale metrics, establishment locations, national-law analysis). Where none of Steps 2-5 applies, a DPO is not mandatory, but Article 37(4) permits a voluntary designation; if one is made voluntarily, Articles 37(5)-(7), 38 and 39 apply in full.
Step 7 — Review triggers. Re-run the assessment on any change of: core processing activities; scale (data-subject numbers, new geographies, new data categories); entry into or exit from a Member State with a headcount trigger; or the addition of a DPIA-triggering processing operation. Because no GDPR headcount exists, growth alone does not create an Article 37(1) obligation — but it can cross a national threshold and it is evidence going to 'large scale'.

6. ROLE-SPECIFIC NOTES
- Processors: Article 37(1) applies to processors in the same terms as to controllers ('The controller and the processor shall designate...'). A processor must run the same Steps 2-5 assessment for its own processing, and should confirm in its customer contracts which party designates where the processor's core activities trigger the obligation.
- Groups: Article 37(2) permits a single DPO for a group of undertakings, provided the DPO is easily accessible from each establishment. Accessibility, not headcount, is the test.
- Independence: Article 38(3) (confirmed in C-534/20, sha256 7a68375c55ca) prohibits instructions, dismissal or penalty for performing DPO tasks, requires direct reporting to the highest management level, and Article 38(5) imposes confidentiality. These attach to the function whatever the trigger for designation.

7. LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
This is a GDPR-level determination, not a jurisdiction-specific legal opinion. It resolves the threshold question asked and identifies the national-law step that must be run for each Member State in which the organisation operates; it does not survey the thresholds of every Member State. The headcount figures appearing above (20 under the current BDSG § 38(1); 10 under the version quoted in C-534/20) are German statutory figures and are expressly not GDPR thresholds. The frequently cited '250 employees' figure is not found in any of the four pages read in full and should not be relied on.

answer:
## 1. Version identified (the document the questionnaire refers to)

- **Document:** Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation **12 December 2024**
- **This version URI:** https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG22-20241212/
- **Latest published version URI:** https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
- Both URIs carry the same text for the points below (identical fetched content, sha256 6e3c5fe39725).

This is a *revision* of WCAG 2.2 (originally a Recommendation on 5 October 2023), not a new guideline version. The WAI FAQ confirms: "On 12 December 2024, we published an update to WCAG 2.2." WCAG 3 is explicitly "years away from being completed," so a December 2024 Recommendation cannot be WCAG 3.

## 2. Ask 1 — Must a page pass 4.1.1 to conform to that version at Level AA?

**Verdict: No.**

Normative basis — WCAG 2.2 §5.2.1 Conformance Level:

> "In order for a web page to conform to WCAG 2.2, all of the following conformance requirements must be satisfied:
> … For Level AA conformance, the web page satisfies all the Level A and Level AA success criteria, or a Level AA conforming alternate version is provided."

And §4.1.1 in the same document:

> "Success Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed)"

The heading is retained for numbering continuity, but the criterion is marked obsolete and removed and its note ends "This criterion no longer has utility and is removed." A removed criterion is not one of "the Level A and Level AA success criteria" that §5.2.1 requires a page to satisfy. Therefore:

- 4.1.1 is **not** a pass/fail conformance gate for WCAG 2.2 Level AA.
- A page can conform to WCAG 2.2 Level AA while containing duplicate IDs or markup that would have failed 4.1.1 under WCAG 2.1, provided the underlying user-facing defects (wrong accessible name, missing role, wrong state, status message not exposed) are absent — those are now caught by other criteria (§1.3.1 Info and Relationships, §4.1.2 Name, Role, Value, §4.1.3 Status Messages, §2.4.4/§2.4.9 Link Purpose, §3.3.2 Labels or Instructions, etc.).
- The correct questionnaire answer is **Not Applicable — 4.1.1 is obsolete and removed in WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024)**, not "Pass" and not "Fail".

Corroborating (informative) W3C pages, useful as an audit exhibit:

- WAI, *What's New in WCAG 2.2*: "The 2.0 and 2.1 success criteria are essentially the same in 2.2, with one exception: 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed from WCAG 2.2."
- WAI, *WCAG 2 FAQ*: "Success Criteria 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete. WCAG 2.2 indicates it as 4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed), along with a note." The same FAQ adds: "(Using tools that assess parsing errors and fixing parsing issues may still be useful — it's just not required for accessibility.)"

## 3. Ask 2 — What does the document say is the reason?

Verbatim note under §4.1.1 in WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024), https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG22-20241212/#parsing:

> "Note
> This criterion was originally adopted to address problems that assistive technology had directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed."

Structured reading of that reason (for the response narrative; the quote above is the citation):

1. **Original purpose** — 4.1.1 existed because AT had to parse HTML directly.
2. **Changed premise** — AT no longer has any need to parse HTML directly (browsers expose a parsed accessibility tree).
3. **Consequence** — the problems 4.1.1 targeted either (a) no longer exist, or (b) are addressed by other success criteria.
4. **Conclusion** — the criterion "no longer has utility and is removed."

The Recommendation does **not** give "it was too hard to test," "vendors complained," or "HTML5 parsing is lenient" as the reason. Do not substitute those; the document's stated reason is the AT-parsing rationale quoted above. (The HTML-parsing-algorithm rationale appears in the WCAG 2.0 *Errata* note and in third-party baselines such as the U.S. Section 508 ICT Testing Baseline, which paraphrases it — cite those only if the questionnaire is scoped to WCAG 2.0/2.1, per §5 below.)

## 4. How to answer the questionnaire as posed (fixed pass/fail format)

Recommended response text for the 4.1.1 row:

> **4.1.1 Parsing — Not Applicable (criterion removed).** WCAG 2.2, W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024 (https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG22-20241212/), lists "Success Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed)" and states: "This criterion was originally adopted to address problems that assistive technology had directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed." Level AA conformance under §5.2.1 requires satisfying all Level A and Level AA success criteria; 4.1.1 is not among them in this version. Our conformance statement is therefore made against the remaining Level A/AA criteria, and parsing-related user impact is reported under 1.3.1, 4.1.2, 4.1.3 and related criteria.

If the form's validation **forces** a binary Pass/Fail (no N/A option), then:

- Answer **Pass**, and attach the N/A note above as the comment/rationale. This is defensible: a criterion that is not a conformance requirement cannot be failed, and no failing condition exists to report. State in the comment that "Pass" is recorded only to satisfy the form's binary validation and is not a claim that 4.1.1 is a live WCAG 2.2 requirement.
- Do **not** answer Fail. There is no basis in WCAG 2.2 for a 4.1.1 failure.
- Do not silently answer Pass without the comment; an auditor reading a bare "Pass" may infer the criterion is still in force and later question why parsing defects were not logged.

Escalation if the customer insists on a 4.1.1 pass/fail *as a requirement*: request that the requirement be re-based either to WCAG 2.2 (drop the row) or explicitly to WCAG 2.1/2.0 (keep the row — see §5).

## 5. Scope caveat — when 4.1.1 *does* still apply

The "No" verdict is specific to the December 2024 WCAG 2.2 Recommendation. It does not hold if the contract or questionnaire is scoped elsewhere:

| Cited standard | Does 4.1.1 exist? | Practical answer |
|---|---|---|
| WCAG 2.2 (REC, 12 Dec 2024) — the case asked about | No — obsolete and removed | Not Applicable; binary fallback = Pass with comment |
| WCAG 2.1 (REC, 5 June 2018, as updated) | Yes (Level A) | Pass — WCAG 2.1/2.0 errata note: "This Success Criteria should be considered as always satisfied for any content using HTML or XML." |
| WCAG 2.0 (REC, 11 Dec 2008, with errata) | Yes (Level A) | Pass — same errata note |
| Section 508 / ICT Testing Baseline (incorporates WCAG 2.0 by reference) | Yes | Pass — baseline test 24.A-Parsing: "No testing necessary" |

Note the direction of inheritance: WCAG 2.2 §Introduction states "Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 also conforms to WCAG 2.0 and WCAG 2.1," and the WAI FAQ states later versions "do not change existing success criteria. One exception is 4.1.1 Parsing." So a WCAG 2.2 conformance claim satisfies a WCAG 2.1/2.0 requirement in practice, and the errata note removes any 4.1.1 exposure there for HTML/XML content.

## 6. Audit defense — evidence to attach

1. Screenshot/PDF of https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG22-20241212/#parsing showing the "(Obsolete and removed)" heading and the note text.
2. Screenshot/PDF of §5.2.1 (Conformance Level) in the same document.
3. Optional corroboration: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/new-in-22/ ("4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed from WCAG 2.2") and https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/faq/ ("Success Criteria 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete…").
4. A one-line pointer in the conformance statement naming the exact version URI and date, since conformance claims must include "Guidelines title, version and URI" and "Conformance level satisfied" (§5.3.1 in WCAG 2.2).

## 7. What the vendor should still test (substitute coverage)

Because 4.1.1 no longer carries the load, verify the user-visible outcomes it used to catch, under their current criteria:

- Duplicate `id` breaking a label/`for` association or `aria-labelledby` → **1.3.1** Info and Relationships, **3.3.2** Labels or Instructions, **4.1.2** Name, Role, Value.
- Bad nesting stripping a role or accessible name → **1.3.1**, **4.1.2**.
- Duplicate attributes corrupting a widget's state → **4.1.2**.
- Dynamically injected status text not announced → **4.1.3** Status Messages.

Report findings under those criteria; do not open 4.1.1 tickets against a WCAG 2.2 target.

answer:
AES-256 per FIPS 197: 14 rounds, 128-bit block, 15 round keys of four words each.

=== 1. Parameters as fixed by FIPS 197 ===
FIPS 197 (NIST, 26 Nov 2001; reaffirmed without technical change by FIPS 197-upd1, May 2023) fixes three parameters: Nb = number of 32-bit words (columns) in the State, Nk = number of 32-bit words in the Cipher Key, Nr = number of rounds.

  | Variant | Nk (words) | Key bits | Nb (words) | Block bits | Nr |
  |---------|-----------|----------|-----------|------------|----|
  | AES-128 |     4     |   128    |     4     |    128     | 10 |
  | AES-192 |     6     |   192    |     4     |    128     | 12 |
  | AES-256 |     8     |   256    |     4     |    128     | 14 |

Source: FIPS 197 Sec. 4.2 and Fig. 4 ('Key-Block-Round Combinations'); identical values in FIPS 197-upd1 Table 3. Quoted: 'Nr = 10 when Nk = 4, Nr = 12 when Nk = 6, and Nr = 14 when Nk = 8' and 'The only Key-Block-Round combinations that conform to this standard are given in Fig. 4.'

=== 2. Ask 2 — rounds used by AES-256: 14 ===
AES-256 is the Nk = 8 instance, therefore Nr = 14. Equivalently, FIPS 197-upd1 states the cipher instantiation directly: 'AES-256(in, key) = CIPHER(in, 14, KEYEXPANSION(key))'. The round count is a parameter of the standard, not an implementation choice: any AES-256 implementation executing 10, 12, or 16 rounds is not AES-256.

=== 3. Ask 3 — block size in bits: 128 ===
The block size is independent of the key length. Quoted: 'For the AES algorithm, the length of the input block, the output block and the State is 128 bits. This is represented by Nb = 4, which reflects the number of 32-bit words (number of columns) in the State.' Also: 'The AES algorithm is capable of using cryptographic keys of 128, 192, and 256 bits to encrypt and decrypt data in blocks of 128 bits.' Nb = 4 for every variant, so AES-256 operates on 16-byte blocks, not 32-byte blocks.

=== 4. Ask 4 — round keys consumed: 15 (each four words) ===
Derivation, from FIPS 197 Sec. 5.1.1 and Sec. 5.2:
  (a) 'Each Round Key consists of Nb words from the key schedule.' With Nb = 4, every round key is an array of exactly four 32-bit words = 128 bits.
  (b) 'The Key Expansion generates a total of Nb (Nr + 1) words: the algorithm requires an initial set of Nb words, and each of the Nr rounds requires Nb words of key data. The resulting key schedule consists of a linear array of 4-byte words, denoted [wi], with i in the range 0 <= i < Nb(Nr + 1).'
  (c) Arithmetic for AES-256: Nb(Nr + 1) = 4 x (14 + 1) = 4 x 15 = 60 words.
  (d) Round keys = words / words-per-round-key = 60 / 4 = Nr + 1 = 15.

The 15 are: the initial AddRoundKey key w[0..3] applied before the first round (round = 0), plus one key w[4r..4r+3] for each of the 14 rounds (1 <= r <= 14). FIPS 197 Sec. 5.1.1: 'In the Cipher, the initial Round Key addition occurs when round = 0, prior to the first application of the round function... The application of the AddRoundKey() transformation to the Nr rounds of the Cipher occurs when 1 <= round <= Nr.' Hence AddRoundKey is invoked exactly Nr + 1 = 15 times, each time with a distinct 128-bit round key.

Cross-check in bits/bytes: 15 round keys x 128 bits = 1920 bits = 240 bytes = 60 32-bit words. This matches the independent statement that AES-256 consumes '15 x 128 = 1920 bits of key material', and matches the Rijndael-256 commentary that 'Rijndael-(256,256) has 14 rounds and 15 round keys (same as with AES-256)'.

=== 5. Convention note that must not be mistaken for an error ===
Some vendor documentation (e.g. the Intel AES-NI whitepaper) says AES-256 'expands the cipher key to 14 round keys'. That is the same object counted differently: it excludes the initial whitening key and treats it as 'Round Key 0', yielding a 0..14 or 1..14 numbering. Under FIPS 197's own definition — a Round Key is a Nb-word value from the key schedule fed to AddRoundKey, and the schedule holds Nb(Nr+1) words — the count is 15. The requested figure ('each an array of four words') is the FIPS 197 count: 15.

=== 6. Scope caveat ===
NIST's December 2024 pre-draft call for comments proposes standardizing a wider-block variant (Rijndael-256, 256-bit block, 256-bit key). That is a separate future algorithm; it is not AES, and it does not alter any value above. AES-256 remains 14 rounds / 128-bit block / 15 four-word round keys.

=== 7. Implementation-facing assertions (Security Engineer view) ===
These three numbers are the ones to pin in code review and in test harnesses; each is checkable mechanically:
  - rounds:      Nr == 14 for key length 32 bytes; reject any other value.
  - block size:  exactly 16 bytes in and out; a 32-byte-block 'AES-256' is Rijndael-256 and is non-conformant.
  - key schedule: len(W) == 4 * (Nr + 1) == 60 words; round_key(r) = W[4r : 4r+4] for r in 0..14; 15 AddRoundKey invocations total.

Two security-relevant consequences worth recording alongside the answer:
  (a) AES-256's key schedule is 240 bytes (60 words), not 176 bytes as for AES-128. Any key-material zeroization routine must wipe the full expanded schedule (240 bytes for AES-256), not just the 32-byte cipher key; under-wiping leaves recoverable key material in memory. Note also that because Nk = 8, FIPS 197 Sec. 5.2 applies the SubWord/RotWord/Rcon transform at every i divisible by Nk = 8 AND an extra SubWord at i ≡ 4 (mod 8) — an AES-256-only branch that AES-128 implementations do not have, and a common source of conformance bugs.
  (b) The 128-bit block fixes the birthday bound at 2^64 blocks (~2^68 bytes) for any mode; mode-level limits (e.g. GCM's ~64 GiB per invocation) must be enforced independently of the 256-bit key strength. A 256-bit key does not raise the block-size-derived limit.

=== 8. Final answer ===
Per FIPS 197: AES-256 uses 14 rounds, operates on a 128-bit block, and consumes 15 round keys, each an array of four 32-bit words (60 key-schedule words, 1920 bits of round-key material).

SOURCE AND READING NOTES
Governing text: NIST Special Publication 800-38D, 'Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC', November 2007. Relevant clauses: §5.2.1.1 (input-data length requirements), §8 (uniqueness requirement, and the 96-bit recommendation), §8.2.2 (RBG-based IV construction), §8.3 (constraints on the number of invocations).
The fetched full text has its superscripts flattened by extraction, so it prints '232', '239-256' and '264' where the standard prints 2^32, 2^39 − 256 and 2^64. The exponents are confirmed two ways: (a) internal arithmetic — '232' appears as the cap whose discussion elsewhere is about 2^64 blocks of data and about a 2^-32 forgery/uniqueness probability, which only closes with 2^32; (b) the 2021 public-comment document on SP 800-38D, which quotes the same sentence as 'shall not exceed 2^32'. All figures below use the true exponents.

ANSWERS

Ask 3 — IV length implementations should restrict support to: 96 bits (12 bytes).
SP 800-38D §8: 'For IVs, it is recommended that implementations restrict support to the length of 96 bits, to promote interoperability, efficiency, and simplicity of design.'
Status of the statement: a recommendation ('is recommended'), not a 'shall'. It is the length a conforming implementation should support — and the only length it need support — for AES-GCM, including under the RBG-based construction. Three consequences worth stating because they are what makes 96 the right restriction:
  • §8.2.2 requires the random field to be at least 96 bits and its length r(i) to be fixed for the life of the key for each supported IV length i. If the only supported length is 96 bits, the whole IV is the random field (direct random string, or the r(i)-bit incrementing function applied to the preceding IV's random field), and the free field is empty. This is the simplest conforming RBG configuration and it is what 'restrict support to 96 bits' buys you.
  • At exactly 96 bits GCM skips the GHASH-based derivation: the IV is used directly as the pre-counter block and the 32-bit incrementing function produces the first counter block. Any other IV length pays a GHASH call per invocation.
  • Restricting to 96 bits does NOT exempt an RBG-based implementation from the §8.3 cap below. §8.3's sole exemption is 'an implementation [that] only uses 96-bit IVs that are generated by the deterministic construction'. RBG-generated 96-bit IVs remain inside the cap.
An implementation may support other IV lengths under the RBG construction (any i with r(i) ≥ 96, random-field length fixed per key, free field arbitrary), but then it must still satisfy the same 2^32 global cap and must fix field lengths per key; supporting only 96 bits is the interoperable, lowest-risk choice the standard points to.

Ask 4 — Maximum total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function under one key: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296.
SP 800-38D §8.3: 'The following requirement applies to all implementations that use either 1) the deterministic construction with IVs whose length is not 96, or 2) the RBG-based construction, for IVs of any length. In other words, unless an implementation only uses 96-bit IVs that are generated by the deterministic construction: The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key.'
Because AES-GCM with RBG-produced IVs is case (2), the cap applies in full. Properties to implement against:
  • It is a shall, not a recommendation, and it is global: summed over every IV length supported and every instance/device/thread holding that key, not per instance.
  • It is the count of authenticated-encryption invocations (i.e. GCM seal/encrypt calls), each invocation regardless of its plaintext size counting as one.
  • The standard shows how to meet it with local limits: e.g. 2^10 devices supporting 64/96/128-bit IVs could be limited to 2^20, 2^21 and 2^20 invocations respectively, summing to 2^32. A single-instance implementation may simply cap at 2^32.
  • §8.3 notes the cap, together with r(i) ≥ 96, is what makes the §8 uniqueness requirement (probability of repeated IV-and-key ≤ 2^-32) hold for the RBG construction.

Ask 5 / Ask 6 — Maximum plaintext length per invocation, in bytes: 68,719,476,704 bytes (= 2^36 − 32).
SP 800-38D §5.2.1.1: 'The bit lengths of the input strings to the authenticated encryption function shall meet the following requirements: • len(P) ≤ 2^39−256; • len(A) ≤ 2^64−1; • 1 ≤ len(IV) ≤ 2^64−1.'
Derivation, exact, no rounding:
  len(P) ≤ 2^39 − 256 bits
  2^39            = 549,755,813,888 bits
  2^39 − 256      = 549,755,813,632 bits
  ÷ 8             = 68,719,476,704 bytes   (2^39 − 256 is divisible by 8: 2^39/8 = 2^36, 256/8 = 32)
  = 2^36 − 32 bytes = 64 GiB − 32 bytes ≈ 68.72 GB ≈ 63.99999997 GiB
  in AES blocks: (2^36 − 32)/16 = 2^32 − 2 = 4,294,967,294 blocks.
This limit is a property of GCM's counter space (the 32-bit counter in inc32 must not wrap into the pre-counter block), so it is independent of the IV construction, of the key, and of the tag length; it applies per invocation, not cumulatively. Related limits from the same clause, for completeness: AAD len(A) ≤ 2^64 − 1 bits; IV 1 ≤ len(IV) ≤ 2^64 − 1 bits.
Cross-check against ask 4 (no internal contradiction): the largest data volume the two limits jointly allow under one key is 2^32 invocations × (2^32 − 2) blocks = 2^64 − 2^33 blocks, which stays below the §9 guidance that 'the total number of blocks of plaintext and AAD that are protected by invocations of the authenticated encryption function during the lifetime of the key should be limited. A reasonable limit for most applications would be 2^64'. The stated per-invocation maximum and per-key invocation maximum are therefore consistent with each other and with §9.

ENFORCEMENT (what an implementation must do)
1. IV length: accept exactly 12 bytes; reject any other length at the API boundary (a 96-bit-only profile). For RBG-based IV generation, draw all 96 bits from an approved RBG of sufficient security strength as the random field (free field empty); optionally derive successors by the 96-bit incrementing function, never repeating an IV under a key.
2. Invocation counter: keep a counter per key (persisted, or guaranteed fresh-key-per-session), increment on every authenticated-encryption call; at 2^32 refuse to encrypt and return an error, requiring a new key. If the key is shared across instances, partition the budget (local limits summing to ≤ 2^32).
3. Plaintext length: reject len(P) > 68,719,476,704 bytes before calling GCM; also reject len(A) > 2^64 − 1 bits and IV length outside [1, 2^64 − 1] bits.
4. Do not rely on the §8.3 exemption unless the implementation uses only 96-bit IVs from the deterministic construction; an RBG-based profile never qualifies.

NOTE ON THE PROOF-OF-ABSENCE PAGES
The harness's proofs of absence for asks 3 and 4 concern only the cryptacular NonceUtil javadoc page (sha256 32ff9db9b2aa), which indeed contains none of '96 bits', 'IV length' or '2^32' and states neither value. That page is not the source of this answer; SP 800-38D itself states both, verbatim, as quoted above. The answer to asks 3 and 4 is therefore not 'the page states none', so no ask is listed in not_stated and no figure is withheld.

## Answer

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts) does **not** require a specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, a specific counting window, or a specific lockout duration. The base control makes all three organization-defined. The requirement is that the organization assign and enforce the values, not that NIST supplies them.

## Authoritative AC-7 text

From NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 / Rev. 5.1, AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS, Control:

> a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
>
> b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.

Discussion excerpt from the same page:

> Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period.

Source: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-53r5.pdf (fetched 2026-11-24T06:03:51Z, sha256 fc63bcd61715). The same AC-7 language appears in the Rev. 5.1 OSCAL PDF at https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Projects/risk-management/800-53%20Downloads/800-53r5/SP_800-53_v5_1-derived-OSCAL.pdf (sha256 9ce01f4d67c9).

## Ask-by-ask disposition

1. **Number of consecutive invalid logon attempts** — No fixed number is required. AC-7(a) contains `[Assignment: organization-defined number]`. The organization must choose the number and document it in the security plan, policy, or equivalent control implementation statement. Result identifier: `organization-defined number`.

2. **Time period within which attempts are counted** — No fixed window is required. AC-7(a) contains `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]`. The organization must choose the counting window and document it. Result identifier: `organization-defined time period`.

3. **Lockout duration** — Not stated on the named page. The full text of the NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 publication at https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-53r5.pdf was searched for `lockout duration`, `account lockout duration`, `duration of the lockout`, and `lockout period`; none of those strings occurs in the 492-page, 1,561,656-character document. The page therefore states no lockout-duration value. The only related AC-7(b) text is a selectable action: `lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]`. That is still an organization-defined parameter, not a NIST-supplied duration, and it is only one of several selectable responses. No figure is given for ask 3.

## What this means for compliance and implementation

AC-7 is satisfied only when the organization has resolved its assignment parameters and implemented them. An unresolved `[Assignment: organization-defined ...]` placeholder is not an implemented control. A compliant implementation statement must at minimum record:

| Parameter | Control location | Required organization decision |
|---|---|---|
| AC-7a count | AC-7(a) | The number of consecutive invalid logon attempts allowed. |
| AC-7a window | AC-7(a) | The time period during which those consecutive attempts are counted. |
| AC-7b response | AC-7(b) | One or more of: temporary lock for an organization-defined time period; lock until administrator release; delay next logon prompt per an organization-defined delay algorithm; notify system administrator; other organization-defined action. |
| AC-7b lock period | AC-7(b), only if the temporary-lock option is selected | The organization-defined time period for the lock. |

The base control does not mandate which AC-7(b) response option must be selected. If the organization selects temporary account/node lock, it must also assign the lock period. If it selects administrator release or a delay algorithm instead, the corresponding organization-defined value or algorithm must be assigned.

NIST SP 800-53B baseline tables include AC-7 in the baselines shown in the fetched baseline workbook, but the baseline file does not supply numeric AC-7 parameter values; the values remain organization-defined. AC-7(1) Automatic Account Lock is listed in the SP 800-53B workbook as incorporated into AC-7, so there is no separate numeric AC-7(1) parameter set to retrieve.

## Direct answer to the question as phrased

- Number: **organization-defined number** — not a NIST-fixed number.
- Time period: **organization-defined time period** — not a NIST-fixed window.
- Lockout duration: **not stated** in the full NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 page; the page provides no duration figure. AC-7(b) exposes a temporary-lock period only as another organization-defined time period if that response option is selected.

# Data checksums in PostgreSQL 18: default state, how to disable, and the pg_upgrade constraint

Scope assumed (state it explicitly to whoever consumes this): a cluster created by stock, unmodified PostgreSQL 18 `initdb` from the upstream distribution. Vendor/package wrappers (Debian `pg_createcluster`, RHEL packaging, container entrypoints, managed-cloud provisioning) may inject flags or pre-create the cluster, so always inspect the real `initdb` command line rather than assuming.

---

## 1. Verdict — bare `initdb` on PostgreSQL 18 enables data checksums

**Yes. Data checksums are ON by default in PostgreSQL 18.** This is a change from PostgreSQL 17 and earlier, where the default was OFF.

Evidence from the PG18 documentation:

- `initdb` reference, option `-k` / `--data-checksums`: *"Use checksums on data pages to help detect corruption by the I/O system that would otherwise be silent. This is enabled by default; use `--no-data-checksums` to disable checksums."*
- Release notes, E.7.2 Migration to Version 18 (incompatibilities): *"Change initdb default to enable data checksums (Greg Sabino Mullane). Checksums can be disabled with the new initdb option `--no-data-checksums`."*
- Section 28.2: *"By default, data pages are protected by checksums, but this can optionally be disabled for a cluster."*

So `initdb -D /pgdata/18/data` with no checksum-related flag produces a cluster with checksums enabled, and `initdb` prints a line saying data page checksums are enabled.

Confirm on the running cluster (three independent checks):

```sql
-- read-only GUC, reflects the cluster-wide setting recorded at initdb / by pg_checksums
SHOW data_checksums;              -- on   (off if disabled)
```

```bash
pg_controldata "$PGDATA" | grep -i checksum
# Data page checksum version: 1     -> checksums enabled
# Data page checksum version: 0     -> checksums disabled
```

Note the setting is cluster-wide only — it cannot be set per database or per table ("Data checksums are enabled or disabled at the full cluster level, and cannot be specified individually for databases or tables"). `data_checksums` is an internal read-only GUC: putting it in `postgresql.conf` makes the server refuse to start ("parameter \"data_checksums\" cannot be changed"). The only supported ways to change it are `initdb` and `pg_checksums`.

---

## 2. How checksums are switched off

There are exactly two supported routes; pick by whether the cluster already exists.

### 2a. At cluster creation (preferred for a new cluster)

Pass the negation flag:

```bash
initdb -D /pgdata/18/data --no-data-checksums
```

- `--no-data-checksums` is the switch that turns checksums off. `-k` / `--data-checksums` still exists and is accepted, but under PG18 it is now redundant (it re-states the default).
- Verify immediately: `initdb` output should say checksums are disabled, `pg_controldata "$PGDATA" | grep -i checksum` shows `Data page checksum version: 0`, and after start `SHOW data_checksums;` returns `off`.
- There is no environment variable or config-file equivalent — the flag is the only knob at creation time. If a wrapper creates the cluster for you, pass the flag through it (e.g. `pg_createcluster 18 main -- --no-data-checksums`, or add it to the container entrypoint's `initdb` invocation), otherwise you inherit the PG18 default of ON.

### 2b. On an existing cluster (offline, with `pg_checksums`)

Checksums can be enabled or disabled later as an **offline** operation:

```bash
# 1. Clean shutdown is mandatory — pg_checksums refuses to run on a running
#    or not-cleanly-shut-down cluster.
pg_ctl -D /pgdata/18/data stop -m fast

# 2. Rewrite every data page without checksums (all databases, all tablespaces).
pg_checksums --disable -D /pgdata/18/data --progress --verbose

# 3. Start and confirm.
pg_ctl -D /pgdata/18/data start
psql -Atc "SHOW data_checksums;"        # off
```

Operational rules and caveats for the DBA running this:

- **Downtime is required.** The server must be stopped and the cluster cleanly shut down; `pg_checksums` will not touch a live or crash-state cluster.
- **It is a full physical rewrite** of every data page in the cluster (all databases and all tablespaces), so it is I/O-heavy and time scales with cluster size. Take a base backup first, and schedule a maintenance window.
- **Cluster-wide only** — it is not a per-database or per-table operation.
- **Idempotent but not free:** running `--disable` on an already-disabled cluster is harmless but still scans the whole cluster.
- **Durability:** `--sync` is on by default; `-N` / `--no-sync` skips the sync and should only be used where you accept that trade-off.
- **Counters are not reset:** checksum failures already accumulated in `pg_stat_database` stay there after the change.
- **Reverse direction** is the same procedure with `pg_checksums --enable`.
- **Alternative if you cannot afford the offline window on the existing cluster:** stand up a new cluster with `initdb --no-data-checksums` and move data with logical replication or dump/restore, then cut over. This costs a migration rather than a rewrite.

---

## 3. What must hold for checksum settings when running `pg_upgrade`

**Constraint: the old cluster and the new cluster must have the same data-checksum setting. `pg_upgrade` compares them and refuses to proceed if they differ.**

Evidence, PG18 release notes E.7.2 (Migration to Version 18, incompatibilities):

> *"Change initdb default to enable data checksums (Greg Sabino Mullane). Checksums can be disabled with the new initdb option `--no-data-checksums`. **pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings**, so this new option can be useful to upgrade non-checksum old clusters."*

Where this is (and is not) documented: the requirement is stated in the PG18 release notes and in the `initdb` reference. The `pg_upgrade` reference page itself does not mention checksums at all — its general statement is that `pg_upgrade` *"will check pg_controldata to make sure all settings are compatible before starting the upgrade."* Checksums are one of those `pg_controldata` settings, so do not go looking for the sentence on the `pg_upgrade` page; the enforcement is real but documented elsewhere.

### The PG18 trap this creates

Before PG18, a bare `initdb` produced checksums OFF. After PG18 it produces checksums ON. So the historically safe recipe — `initdb` the new cluster with no special flags, upgrade a PG17-or-earlier cluster — now produces a **mismatch** and `pg_upgrade` aborts before transferring anything.

| Old cluster | New PG18 cluster created with | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| checksums OFF (typical ≤ PG17) | bare `initdb` (checksums ON — the new default) | **MISMATCH — upgrade refused.** This is the PG18 trap. |
| checksums OFF | `initdb --no-data-checksums` | OK |
| checksums OFF | `pg_checksums --enable` on the old cluster first, then bare `initdb` | OK |
| checksums ON | bare `initdb` | OK |
| checksums ON | `initdb --no-data-checksums` | **MISMATCH — upgrade refused.** |

### Procedure for the common case (≤ PG17 old cluster, checksums off)

```bash
# Pre-flight: this fails fast on the mismatch, before any file movement.
/usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_upgrade --check \
  -b /usr/pgsql-17/bin -B /usr/pgsql-18/bin \
  -d /pgdata/17/data -D /pgdata/18/data

# Option A — keep the old cluster untouched, disable checksums on the new one.
initdb -D /pgdata/18/data --no-data-checksums

# Option B — keep checksums going forward by enabling them on the old cluster first.
pg_ctl -D /pgdata/17/data stop -m fast
pg_checksums --enable -D /pgdata/17/data --progress --verbose
pg_ctl -D /pgdata/17/data start     # then shut down again for the upgrade itself
```

How to choose:

- **Option A** is fast and preserves the status quo (no checksums after the upgrade). Correct when the absence of checksums is a deliberate decision (e.g. write-throughput-sensitive workload) or when the offline window on the old cluster is unavailable.
- **Option B** costs one full offline rewrite of the old cluster but leaves you with checksums enabled post-upgrade. This is the recommended long-term choice: PG18's default is ON, silent I/O corruption detection is the whole point of the feature, and the per-page write cost is small. Doing it now avoids carrying a legacy off-cluster forward and hitting the same decision at the next major upgrade.

Do not attempt to resolve the mismatch by editing `postgresql.conf` on either cluster — `data_checksums` cannot be changed there. It is `initdb` or `pg_checksums` only.

---

## 4. Verification checklist

Run before and after any change, and before the real upgrade run:

1. `pg_controldata "$PGDATA" | grep -i checksum` → `Data page checksum version: 1` (on) or `0` (off), on **both** clusters.
2. `psql -Atc "SHOW data_checksums;"` on each running cluster.
3. `pg_upgrade --check ...` completes without a checksum-settings complaint; only then run the real upgrade.
4. After the upgrade, start the new cluster and re-run (2) to confirm the setting carried over as intended.

## 5. Out of scope / assumptions to confirm

- Upstream PG18 behaviour is assumed. Vendor builds and managed services may pre-create the cluster or wrap `initdb`; confirm with `SHOW data_checksums;` on the actual instance rather than trusting the default.
- If both clusters are PG18, they were created under the same default and match automatically unless someone explicitly passed a checksum flag or ran `pg_checksums` on one of them.
- Enabling checksums has a small ongoing write-performance cost and per-page storage cost; disabling is a legitimate deliberate choice, but it should be a recorded decision, not an accident of a default that changed under you.

# Which kubelets are inside the supported skew for a v1.27 kube-apiserver

## Answer

**Only kubelet v1.25.** Of the three candidates, v1.25 is the single version inside the Kubernetes version skew policy for a kube-apiserver at v1.27.

| kubelet | Gap to apiserver (minor) | Governing rule | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1.28 | +1 (newer) | "kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver" | **Outside** — kubelet is newer than the apiserver |
| v1.25 | 2 older | up to 3 minors older (1.25 is not < 1.25, so the 3-minor rule applies) | **Inside** — exactly on the inclusive floor |
| v1.24 | 3 older | kubelet < 1.25 is limited to 2 minors older | **Outside** — 3 > 2 |

Supported set for a 1.27 apiserver: **{1.25, 1.26, 1.27}**. Candidates inside it: **v1.25 only**.

## Policy text used (kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/, fetched 2026-11-24T06:08:41Z)

Under the heading *kubelet*:

1. "kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver."
2. "kubelet may be up to three minor versions older than kube-apiserver (kubelet < 1.25 may only be up to two minor versions older than kube-apiserver)."
3. "Example: kube-apiserver is at 1.37, kubelet is supported at 1.37, 1.36, 1.35, and 1.34" — i.e. the floor is inclusive and is apiserver_minor − 3.

Scope note from the same page: "This document describes the maximum version skew supported between various Kubernetes components. Specific cluster deployment tools may place additional restrictions on version skew."

## Formalisation (the rule as an executable predicate)

Let `A` = kube-apiserver minor, `K` = kubelet minor (patch ignored; the policy is expressed in minor versions only).

```
allowed(K, A) := (K <= A)                                        # kubelet not newer
             and ( (K >= 1.25 and K >= A - 3)                    # general 3-minor window
                   or (K <  1.25 and K >= A - 2) )               # pre-1.25 carve-out: 2 minors
```

Equivalently, the supported kubelet window for a given apiserver is:

```
floor(A) = max(1.25, A - 3)      # for A >= 28 the 3-minor floor dominates
           A - 2                 # only when that value is < 1.25
ceiling(A) = A                   # inclusive; kubelet may not be newer
```

For `A = 27`: `A - 3 = 24`, but 24 < 1.25, so the carve-out requires `K >= 25`; the 3-minor branch requires `K >= 1.25`. Both branches therefore bottom out at **1.25**, and the ceiling is **1.27**. Window = **[1.25, 1.27]**.

```python
# Reference implementation of the policy check (kubelet vs kube-apiserver).
def kubelet_supported(kubelet_minor: int, apiserver_minor: int) -> bool:
    if kubelet_minor > apiserver_minor:
        return False                       # kubelet must not be newer
    if kubelet_minor < 25:
        return kubelet_minor >= apiserver_minor - 2   # <1.25: at most 2 minors older
    return kubelet_minor >= apiserver_minor - 3       # >=1.25: at most 3 minors older

# A = 27
# kubelet_supported(28, 27) -> False  (newer)
# kubelet_supported(25, 27) -> True   (gap 2, within 3)
# kubelet_supported(24, 27) -> False  (gap 3, but <1.25 caps it at 2)
```

## Per-candidate derivation

**v1.28 against v1.27.** `K > A`. The first sentence of the kubelet rule is absolute and has no exception: a kubelet may never be newer than the kube-apiserver it talks to. This is the direction that matters operationally — an apiserver does not have to accept API features or node-status fields introduced by a newer kubelet. **Outside.**

**v1.25 against v1.27.** Gap = 27 − 25 = 2 minor versions older. `K = 25` is *not* `< 1.25`, so the parenthetical carve-out does not apply and the general three-minor window governs. 2 ≤ 3. The kubelet is not newer. **Inside** — and this is the boundary case, one minor above the floor of 1.25.

**v1.24 against v1.27.** Gap = 27 − 24 = 3 minor versions older. Read alone, the three-minor rule would admit it. But `K = 24 < 1.25`, so the carve-out binds and the tolerance shrinks to two minor versions; 3 > 2. **Outside.** This is the trap in the question: 1.24 is exactly n−3, which looks inside the headline rule but is excluded by the exception for pre-1.25 kubelets.

## Edge semantics that decide this case

- **The carve-out threshold is on the kubelet version, not the apiserver version.** "kubelet < 1.25 may only be up to two minor versions older" — a 1.24 kubelet is governed by the two-minor limit regardless of how new the apiserver is. A 1.25 kubelet is not covered by the carve-out even when paired with a much newer apiserver.
- **The floor is inclusive.** "up to three minor versions older" includes exactly three; "up to two" includes exactly two. A kubelet exactly at the tolerated boundary is supported, so the only question for 1.24 is whether the boundary is 2 or 3, and the carve-out makes it 2.
- **The ceiling is inclusive but one-sided.** `K = A` is supported; `K = A + 1` is not. There is no "kubelet may be one newer" allowance (unlike kubectl, which is ±1).
- **HA narrows, never widens.** "If version skew exists between kube-apiserver instances in an HA cluster, this narrows the allowed kubelet versions." If this cluster ran apiservers at both 1.27 and 1.26, the ceiling would drop to 1.26 and the window would become {1.25, 1.26} — 1.25 stays inside, so the answer to the question is unchanged.
- **Upgrade/downgrade does not change the window, only the order you walk it.** The supported upgrade order is apiserver first, then controller-manager/scheduler/cloud-controller-manager, then kubelets and kube-proxy; during that walk the kubelet must remain inside [apiserver−3 (or −2), apiserver].

## Robustness of the verdict

The n−2 vs n−3 history does not change the answer. Under the older rule (kubelet up to two minor versions older, no carve-out) a 1.27 apiserver admits {1.25, 1.26, 1.27} — identical to the current rule's result. So for these three candidates the verdict is invariant to which generation of the rule is applied; only the *reason* for excluding v1.24 changes (carve-out under the current text, the flat two-minor limit under the older text). v1.28 and v1.25 are decided by clauses that have never changed.

## Premises and caveats to state alongside the answer

- **Reference policy:** the upstream Kubernetes version skew policy at kubernetes.io, not a vendor-modified matrix. Managed distributions (EKS, GKE, AKS) publish their own support windows and may be stricter or longer-lived; if this cluster is managed, re-check against the provider's calendar before acting.
- **Single apiserver minor version assumed.** If the control plane is skewed (e.g. 1.27 and 1.26 instances), apply the HA narrowing above; the answer for v1.25 still holds.
- **Skew is not support lifetime.** The policy page states the project maintains the most recent three minor releases (1.37, 1.36, 1.35 at fetch time). A v1.27 apiserver is outside that maintenance window, so while the *skew* verdict above is correct, a cluster on 1.27 is past end of life for patches and should be upgraded. Skew compliance and release support are two different checks; this answer addresses only the former.
- **Only kubelet↔kube-apiserver is in scope.** kube-proxy (3 minors older, not newer, plus ±3 against the kubelet on its node), control-plane components (1 minor older, not newer) and kubectl (±1) have their own rules and are not covered by this verdict.

## Reproduce the check

```bash
# On any node, read the two versions and compare minors:
kubectl version -o json | jq -r '.serverVersion.minor'   # apiserver minor -> 27
kubelet --version                                        # e.g. v1.25.x -> 25
# Apply kubelet_supported(kubelet_minor, apiserver_minor) from above.
```

Expected outputs for the three candidates with `apiserver_minor = 27`: `28 -> false`, `25 -> true`, `24 -> false`.
