RFC 9293, Section 3.7.1 (Maximum Segment Size Option) — normative answer

Verbatim specification (RFC 9293 §3.7.1, requirement MUST-15):

  "If an MSS Option is not received at connection setup, TCP implementations
   MUST assume a default send MSS of 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60)
   for IPv6 (MUST-15)."

And in the RFC's own requirement-status table (§4 / implementation checklist):

  | Requirement                    | Level   |
  |--------------------------------+---------|
  | IPv4 Send-MSS default is 536   | MUST-15 |
  | IPv6 Send-MSS default is 1220  | MUST-15 |

1. Answers to the asks

  Ask 1 (constraint): the rule applies when the connection is established — i.e., SYN / SYN,ACK exchange completed — and the peer's SYN (or SYN,ACK) carried no MSS option at all. It is the *send* MSS that is defaulted; the local receive MSS is unaffected.

  Ask 2 (IPv4 default send MSS): 536 octets.
  (Same section, for completeness of the original question: IPv6 default send MSS = 1220 octets.)

  Ask 3 (requirement level): MUST — a mandatory requirement, tagged MUST-15 in RFC 9293's requirement numbering. It is not a SHOULD, not a MAY, and not merely a recommended default.

2. Where the numbers come from (derivation, for review)

  IPv4: 576 octets  = minimum IPv4 reassembly buffer size (RFC 791 / RFC 1122).
        - 20 octets  = IPv4 header (no options)
        - 20 octets  = TCP header (no options)
        = 536 octets of TCP payload  ->  576 - 40 = 536.  Checks.

  IPv6: 1280 octets = IPv6 minimum MTU / minimum reassembly buffer (RFC 8200).
        - 40 octets  = IPv6 fixed header (no extension headers)
        - 20 octets  = TCP header (no options)
        = 1220 octets of TCP payload  ->  1280 - 60 = 1220.  Checks.

  Note the asymmetry: 40 vs 60 subtracted is deliberate and correct — the IPv6 base header is 40 octets versus IPv4's 20, so the IPv6 default is 1280-60, not 1280-40.

3. How this sits with the neighbouring MSS requirements (do not conflate them)

  - MUST-14: a TCP endpoint MUST implement both sending and receiving the MSS Option.
  - SHLD-5: an endpoint SHOULD send an MSS Option in every SYN when its *receive* MSS differs from the default 536 (IPv4) / 1220 (IPv6); MAY-3: it MAY send it always.
  - MUST-15 (the answer here): if no MSS Option is received at connection setup, the endpoint MUST assume the default *send* MSS of 536 (IPv4) / 1220 (IPv6).
  - MUST-16: the *effective* send MSS must then be the smaller of the send MSS and the largest size the IP layer permits:
        Eff.snd.MSS = min(SendSMS + 20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize
    with, as the RFC states, "SendSMS ... the MSS value received from the remote host, or the default 536 for IPv4 or 1220 for IPv6, if no MSS Option is received."
  - MUST-67: an MSS value that *is* sent must be based on the local receive buffer (MMS_R), not on this default.
  - SHLD-6: the MSS in effect should account for varying path MTU (PMTUD/PLPMTUD), which can reduce — never raise — the value used per path.

  Sanity check of the arithmetic in the effective-MSS formula: with SendSMS = 536, no IP options, TCPhdrsize = 20, and any MMS_S >= 556, Eff.snd.MSS = min(556, MMS_S) - 20 = 536. The default is therefore self-consistent and never exceeded by its own formula. A 536-octet send MSS corresponds to a 576-octet IPv4 datagram (536 + 20 TCP + 20 IP) and a 1220-octet send MSS to a 1280-octet IPv6 packet (1220 + 20 TCP + 40 IPv6), i.e. exactly the minimum reassembly/MTU figures — no segment produced under this default can exceed them.

  Historical caution: RFC 879's older wording ("if this option is not used, any segment size is allowed") is superseded. Under RFC 9293 the 536/1220 default is MUST-level, so an endpoint may not fall back to "anything goes" when the option is absent.

4. Implementation procedure (directly applicable)

  On connection setup, per connection, per address family:

    function initial_send_mss(family, received_mss_option):
        if received_mss_option is present:
            send_mss = received_mss_option.value          # MUST-14 (receive side)
        else if family == AF_INET:
            send_mss = 536                                # MUST-15
        else if family == AF_INET6:
            send_mss = 1220                               # MUST-15
        else:
            error("no MSS default defined for this family")
        return send_mss

    function effective_send_mss(send_mss, mms_s, tcp_hdr_size, ip_option_size):
        return min(send_mss + 20, mms_s) - tcp_hdr_size - ip_option_size   # MUST-16

  Worked example (IPv4, peer sent no MSS, no IP options, MMS_S = 1500-20):
    send_mss   = 536                                     # MUST-15
    eff.snd.MSS = min(536+20, 1480) - 20 - 0 = min(556,1480) - 20 = 536
    -> each data segment carries at most 536 octets of TCP payload.

  Worked example (IPv6, peer sent no MSS, no extension headers, MMS_S = 1280-40):
    send_mss   = 1220                                    # MUST-15
    eff.snd.MSS = min(1220+20, 1240) - 20 - 0 = 1220

5. Conformance checklist entries to record

  [ ] MUST-15 (IPv4): when no MSS option is received at connection setup, assume send MSS = 536 octets.   PASS criterion: segment payload never exceeds 536 on such a connection unless reduced further by MUST-16/PMTUD.
  [ ] MUST-15 (IPv6): when no MSS option is received at connection setup, assume send MSS = 1220 octets.  PASS criterion: segment payload never exceeds 1220 on such a connection unless reduced further by MUST-16/PMTUD.
  [ ] MUST-16: effective send MSS computed as min(SendSMS+20, MMS_S) - TCPhdrsize - IPoptionsize and never larger than the MUST-15 default when that default is in force.
  [ ] MUST-14: sending and receiving the MSS Option both implemented, so the default only ever applies on the genuine no-option path.

# Maximum permitted exposure at 93 dBA and the L(ex,8) ceiling — COHSR Part VII

## 1. Governing instrument and scope (ask 1)

Canada Occupational Health and Safety Regulations, SOR/86-304, **Part VII (Levels of Sound)**, made under Part II of the Canada Labour Code and administered by the federal Labour Program (ESDC). Consolidation relied on: SOR/86-304 as currently in force (current to 2026-10-29; last amended 2025-03-26), ss. 7.1–7.8 and the Part VII schedule, read as quoted in the sources for this task.

Excluded by the request and not relied on here: the Maritime Occupational Health and Safety Regulations (SOR/2010-120) and the Canada Oil and Gas Occupational Safety and Health Regulations (SOR/87-612). If the work place is a vessel or an offshore installation, those instruments (and their own noise provisions) govern instead and the numbers below do not apply.

## 2. The two separate limits in s. 7.4

Section 7.4 (verbatim, in force):

> **7.4** No employee in a work place shall, in any 24 hour period, be exposed to
> (a) an A-weighted sound pressure level set out in column I of the schedule for a duration of exposure exceeding the applicable duration set out in column II, or
> (b) a noise exposure level (Lex 8) that exceeds 87 dBA.

These are **two independent requirements**, both of which must be met in the same 24-hour period:

- **(a) a per-level duration cap** — read from the Part VII schedule; this is the limit the 93 dBA question is asking about;
- **(b) a dose cap** — the 8-hour-normalised noise exposure level L(ex,8) must not exceed **87 dBA**, regardless of how the exposure is distributed.

Satisfying (a) alone is not sufficient: other exposure in the same 24 hours (measured and counted down to 74 dBA per s. 7.2(3)) can push L(ex,8) over 87 dBA even when no single level exceeds its column II duration.

## 3. The per-level duration cap at 93 dBA (ask 2)

The Part VII schedule is headed, in column II, "Maximum duration of exposure in hours per employee per 24 hour period", with column I giving the A-weighted sound pressure level from 87 dBA to 120 dBA. It is built on a criterion level of 87 dBA for 8 hours and a **3 dB exchange rate**:

  T(L) = 8 / 2^((L − 87)/3)   hours per 24-hour period

Schedule values (column I → column II):

| dBA | h/24 h | dBA | h/24 h |
|---|---|---|---|
| 87 | 8.0 | 99 | 0.50 |
| 88 | 6.4 | 100 | 0.40 |
| 89 | 5.0 | 101 | 0.32 |
| 90 | 4.0 | 102 | 0.25 |
| 91 | 3.2 | 103 | 0.20 |
| 92 | 2.5 | 104 | 0.16 |
| **93** | **2.0** | 105 | 0.13 |
| 94 | 1.6 | 106 | 0.10 |
| 95 | 1.3 | 107 | 0.080 |
| 96 | 1.0 | 108 | 0.064 |
| 97 | 0.80 | 109 | 0.050 |
| 98 | 0.64 | 110 | 0.040 |
|   |   | 111–120 | 0.032 → 0.004 |

At L = 93 dBA:

  T = 8 / 2^((93 − 87)/3) = 8 / 2^2 = 8 / 4 = **2.0 hours**

**Answer to ask 2: 2.0 hours (120 minutes) per employee per 24-hour period** is the longest permitted exposure to a steady 93 dBA. Exposure for longer than 2.0 h at 93 dBA in any 24-hour period contravenes s. 7.4(a).

## 4. The separate L(ex,8) ceiling (ask 3)

s. 7.1 defines noise exposure level (Lex,8) as "10 times the logarithm to the base 10 of the time integral over any 24 hour period of a squared A-weighted sound pressure divided by 8, the reference sound pressure being 20 µPa" — i.e. the 8-hour-normalised (equal-energy) level. s. 7.4(b) caps it:

**Answer to ask 3: L(ex,8) shall not exceed 87 dBA.**

ESDC IPG-074 states the same thing in plain terms: paragraph 7.4(b) "prescribes that the noise exposure level (Lex, 8) of an employee shall not exceed 87 dBA for 8 hours in any 24-hour period."

## 5. Internal consistency check (why 2.0 h and 87 dBA agree)

For a steady 93 dBA held for the full permitted 2.0 h:

  L(ex,8) = 93 + 10·log10(2.0 / 8) = 93 − 6.02 = **86.98 dBA ≈ 87.0 dBA**

That is **exactly at** the 87 dBA ceiling, not above it — the schedule is constructed so that the full column II duration at any tabulated level yields L(ex,8) = 87.0 dBA (e.g. 96 dBA × 1.0 h → 96 − 9.03 = 86.97 dBA; 90 dBA × 4.0 h → 90 − 3.01 = 86.99 dBA). Therefore:

- 2.0 h at 93 dBA satisfies **both** s. 7.4(a) and s. 7.4(b);
- any duration **greater than 2.0 h** at 93 dBA breaches **both** provisions simultaneously;
- the two answers are mutually consistent and neither stated value violates a limit set elsewhere in this deliverable.

## 6. Applying it when 93 dBA is not the only exposure in the 24 hours

Use the dose-fraction method against the 87 dBA / 8 h criterion (3 dB exchange rate):

  Dose D = Σ (C_i / T_i), where T_i = 8 / 2^((L_i − 87)/3)

Compliance requires **D ≤ 1.0** (equivalently L(ex,8) ≤ 87 dBA), and each individual C_i ≤ T_i (s. 7.4(a)).

Time remaining at 93 dBA after other exposures:

  C_93,max = 2.0 × (1.0 − D_other) hours

Worked example: 4.0 h at 88 dBA → D = 4.0 / 6.4 = 0.625; remaining dose 0.375; allowable time at 93 dBA = 0.375 × 2.0 = **0.75 h (45 min)**, not 2.0 h.

Note s. 7.2(3): measurement and calculation of L(ex,8) must take into account A-weighted levels of **74 dBA and greater** (levels below 74 dBA may also be included, s. 7.2(4)); measurement is per CSA CAN/CSA-Z107.56-13 clauses referenced in s. 7.2.

## 7. Reading a measured level that falls between table rows

The schedule tabulates discrete levels only. For a measured steady level that is not a tabulated value (e.g. 93.4 dBA), the defensible practice is to use the next **higher** tabulated level (94 dBA → 1.6 h), which is conservative and, in any event, the s. 7.4(b) dose cap of 87 dBA L(ex,8) remains the binding overall constraint and is calculated exactly from the measured level and time.

## 8. Other Part VII duties triggered at 93 dBA (context, not part of the two answers)

- **s. 7.3** — where an employee may be exposed to ≥ 84 dBA for a duration likely to endanger hearing, the employer must, without delay, appoint a qualified person to investigate the degree of exposure and notify the work place committee / health and safety representative; the report is kept 10 years and, where L(ex,8) ≥ 84 dBA is likely, posted with written hazard information to employees.
- **s. 7.5** — reduction of exposure (engineering/administrative controls) where the s. 7.4 limits would be exceeded.
- **s. 7.6** — hearing protectors, including for employees whose L(ex,8) is ≥ 84 dBA and ≤ 87 dBA where recommended, and mandatory use where the limits are exceeded. **Hearing protection does not relax s. 7.4**: the limits are on the employee's exposure, and protectors are an additional control, not a licence to extend the 2.0 h.
- **s. 7.8** — signs warning of a potentially hazardous level of sound must be posted at conspicuous locations where an employee may be exposed to > 87 dBA.

## 9. Impulsive sound

Part VII of the general federal Regulations contains **no separate peak/impulse limit** (the CCOHS jurisdictional table lists "—" for Canada (Federal) impulse/impact limits; the 140 dB peak limits shown there are provincial/territorial, e.g. BC, Quebec, New Brunswick, and do not apply to federal work places). If the 93 dBA contains impulsive components, the L(ex,8) and per-level limits above still govern; the provincial peak limits should not be imported into a federal work place.

## 10. Bottom line

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Longest permitted exposure to a steady 93 dBA, per employee per 24-hour period (COHSR s. 7.4(a) + Part VII schedule, 3 dB exchange rate) | **2.0 hours (120 min)** |
| Separate ceiling on the 8-hour-normalised noise exposure level L(ex,8) (COHSR s. 7.4(b)) | **87 dBA** |

At 2.0 h and 93 dBA the resulting L(ex,8) is 86.98 dBA — at, not over, the 87 dBA ceiling.

question: X32
shape: Occupational noise, Great Britain statutory instrument
answer:
# Occupational hygiene note: statutory noise values (GB) and the treatment of hearing-protector attenuation

**Prepared for:** manufacturing employer, Great Britain
**Legal basis:** Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 (SI 2005/1643), in particular regulation 4; HSE guidance INDG362 and the HSE noise pages.
**Status of this note:** the values and the legal rule below are fixed by the Regulations and do not depend on site data. The worked example in section 4 uses illustrative figures to show the arithmetic; it is not a substitute for a site assessment.

---

## 1. The statutory values (regulation 4)

| Statutory value | Daily or weekly personal noise exposure (L_EP,d / L_EP,w) | Peak sound pressure (L_Cpeak) |
|---|---|---|
| **Lower exposure action value** — reg 4(1) | **80 dB(A)** | **135 dB(C)** |
| **Upper exposure action value** — reg 4(2) | **85 dB(A)** | **137 dB(C)** |
| **Exposure limit value** — reg 4(3) | **87 dB(A)** | **140 dB(C)** |

### 1.1 Which of these are the 'legal exposure limit values'

'Exposure limit value' is a defined term in reg 2: *"the level of daily or weekly personal noise exposure or of peak sound pressure set out in regulation 4 which must not be exceeded"*. The exposure limit values are therefore **87 dB(A)** and **140 dB(C)**. Reg 6(4) puts the duty plainly: the employer must ensure employees are not exposed above an exposure limit value, and if one is exceeded must **forthwith** reduce exposure below it, identify the reason, and modify the organisational and technical measures to prevent recurrence.

The 80/85 dB(A) and 135/137 dB(C) figures are **action values**, not limit values: they are trigger points for specific duties. They are given above because the employer's second question concerns the upper action value, and because in practice the whole ladder has to be applied together. No number in this note contradicts another: 80 < 85 < 87 dB(A) and 135 < 137 < 140 dB(C).

### 1.2 Daily versus weekly averaging

- **L_EP,d (daily personal noise exposure)** is the default basis.
- **L_EP,w (weekly personal noise exposure)** may be used *in place of* L_EP,d **only where the employee's exposure varies markedly from day to day** (reg 4(4)), calculated for a nominal 5-day week (Schedule 1 Part 2).
- Whichever averaging period is chosen applies to **both** the action values and the exposure limit values. Weekly averaging is not a device for diluting a consistently noisy week.
- Exposure covers **all** noise in the working day/week — the noisy task plus the quieter periods, other areas walked through, and noise from other people's work.

### 1.3 Peak sound pressure

'Peak sound pressure' is the **maximum** sound pressure to which the employee is exposed, ascertained per Schedule 2, expressed C-weighted as L_Cpeak = 20 lg(p_Cpeak / 20 µPa). It is a single-figure, instantaneous criterion — it is **not** averaged over the day or week, and it is not interchangeable with the A-weighted average. It matters most for impact and impulsive noise (presses, ejection of parts, hammer blows, gas release, door slams).

### 1.4 Commencement

The Regulations came into force on 6 April 2006 generally, and 6 April 2008 for the music and entertainment sectors. Both dates are long spent; **no transitional provision applies** to a manufacturing employer. (Equivalent Northern Ireland Regulations carry the same numerical values; if any site is in Northern Ireland, the numbers in section 1 are unchanged.)

---

## 2. May hearing-protector attenuation be counted against the upper exposure action value?

### 2.1 Verdict: **No.**

Regulation 4(5) states:

> *"In applying the exposure limit values in paragraph (3), but not in applying the lower and upper exposure action values in paragraphs (1) and (2), account shall be taken of the protection given to the employee by any personal hearing protectors provided by the employer in accordance with regulation 7(2)."*

HSE guidance is to the same effect (INDG362): *"Do not make any allowance for the wearing of personal hearing protection when you estimate workers' noise exposure levels."* And regulation 6(3) requires the programme of organisational and technical measures at or above the upper exposure action value to be established **"excluding the provision of personal hearing protectors"**.

### 2.2 What that means operationally

1. **Action-value judgements are made on unprotected exposure.** Decide whether 80/85 dB(A) or 135/137 dB(C) is reached or exceeded from the measured or reliably estimated noise exposure **with no deduction for hearing protectors** — even if everyone in the area wears them correctly and every day.
2. **Hearing protection is not a control measure for the purposes of the upper action value.** At or above 85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C) the employer must establish and implement a programme of organisational and technical measures (reg 6(3)) — engineering control, reduced exposure time, work scheduling, maintenance — and designate Hearing Protection Zones. Protection is *additional to* that programme, not a substitute for it (reg 7, INDG362: "You should not use hearing protection as an alternative to controlling noise by technical and organisational means").
3. **The only place protector attenuation enters the arithmetic is the exposure limit value check** — 87 dB(A) and 140 dB(C) — and only for protectors *provided* by the employer in accordance with reg 7(2).
4. **Credit is for the protection actually given, not the laboratory rating.** The reg 4(5) wording is "the protection given to the employee". Real-world fit, wearing time and condition reduce it. The employer must be able to show protectors are worn fully and properly (fitting checks, supervision, maintenance/replacement), or the ELV calculation rests on a fiction.
5. **If protection is issued but not worn, there is no credit at all** — and the exposure limit value is then being exceeded.
6. **If the exposure limit value is exceeded even after crediting protection**, reg 6(4) applies immediately: reduce below the limit forthwith, find the cause, change the measures.
7. **For impulsive noise, do not lean on protection.** Legally the credit is available against the 140 dB(C) peak limit, but attenuation at a millisecond-scale peak is poorly characterised and easily defeated by fit and by the protector's recovery behaviour. A measured L_Cpeak above 140 dB(C) should be treated as requiring an engineering fix (silencing, damping the ejection, changing the process), not a bigger earplug.

### 2.3 Worked statement of the rule

| Question being asked | Use measured exposure | Deduct protector attenuation? |
|---|---|---|
| Has the lower action value (80 dB(A) / 135 dB(C)) been reached? | Yes | **No** |
| Has the upper action value (85 dB(A) / 137 dB(C)) been reached? | Yes | **No** |
| Is the exposure limit value (87 dB(A) / 140 dB(C)) complied with? | Yes | **Yes** — protection provided under reg 7(2), as worn |

---

## 3. Procedure — how to reach the values correctly

**Step 1 — Group exposures.** Define groups of employees with similar exposure (by task, area, machine and shift), not by job title. A press shop, a finishing area and a packing line are different groups even if staff rotate.

**Step 2 — Measure or reliably estimate.** Obtain L_Aeq,T for each task/segment and the L_Cpeak for the day. Personal dosimetry or calibrated sound-level measurement combined with exposure times. Instruments to Class 1, calibration checked before and after. Measure the **noise in the workplace** — never measure inside or behind a protector to derive exposure.

**Step 3 — Compute L_EP,d** (Schedule 1 Part 1):

- Single segment: `L_EP,d = L_Aeq,Te + 10 lg(Te / 8)` with Te in hours.
- Several segments: `L_EP,d = 10 lg[ (1/8) × Σ Ti × 10^(0.1 × L_Aeq,i) ]` with Ti in hours.

**Step 4 — Weekly averaging, only if justified** (reg 4(4), Schedule 1 Part 2):

`L_EP,w = 10 lg[ (1/5) × Σ(i=1..m) 10^(0.1 × L_EP,d,i) ]` for the m days in the week on which the person is exposed.

**Step 5 — Determine L_Cpeak** for the day: `L_Cpeak = 20 lg(p_Cpeak / 20 µPa)`, taking the highest peak to which the employee is exposed.

**Step 6 — Compare the UNPROTECTED values** with 80/85 dB(A) and 135/137 dB(C) and write down which duties are triggered: risk assessment and information/instruction/training at 80; the reg 6(3) control programme excluding HPD, Hearing Protection Zones, provision and mandatory use of protectors, and health surveillance at 85.

**Step 7 — Only now, and only if the unprotected L_EP,d ≥ 87 dB(A) or L_Cpeak ≥ 140 dB(C), do the exposure limit value check:**
- Determine the required attenuation: `required attenuation = L_EP,d − 87` (and `L_Cpeak − 140` for the peak).
- Select the protector and calculate protected exposure using a recognised method (octave-band assumed-protection method preferred; HML or SNR methods for screening only), using the manufacturer's declared data for the actual model issued.
- Compare protected exposure with 87 dB(A) / 140 dB(C). If still above, reg 6(4) applies immediately.

**Step 8 — Record.** Exposure values and averaging period, measurement method and dates, the group assessed, the protectors issued and the basis of selection, and an explicit statement that **action-value determinations were made without credit for hearing protection**. Record the findings and the action taken or intended (reg 5).

---

## 4. Worked example (illustrative figures)

A press operator works 6 hours at a press where L_Aeq = 93 dB(A), and 2 hours elsewhere at 80 dB(A). The press ejects parts with a measured L_Cpeak of 143 dB(C). Protectors issued: an earplug declared SNR 25 dB and an earmuff declared SNR 30 dB.

**A-weighted exposure**
- Press segment: 93 + 10 lg(6/8) = 93 − 1.25 = 91.75 dB(A)
- Other segment: 80 + 10 lg(2/8) = 80 − 6.02 = 73.98 dB(A)
- Combined: 10 lg(10^9.175 + 10^7.398) = 10 lg(1.521 × 10^9) = **91.8 dB(A)**

**Peak:** **143 dB(C)**

**Step 6 — unprotected comparison (no deduction for protectors):**
- 91.8 dB(A) exceeds the lower action value (80), the upper action value (85) and the exposure limit value (87).
- 143 dB(C) exceeds the lower (135) and upper (137) action values and the 140 dB(C) limit.

Therefore, irrespective of the protectors: risk assessment, information/instruction/training, the reg 6(3) programme of organisational and technical measures (excluding HPD), a designated Hearing Protection Zone, provision of protectors with mandatory use, and health surveillance are all required. **None of these duties is displaced by the fact that the protectors reduce exposure to a comfortable level.**

**Step 7 — exposure limit value check (the only place protection counts):**
- Required attenuation, A-weighted: 91.8 − 87 = **4.8 dB**.
- Required attenuation, peak: 143 − 140 = **3 dB**.
- Both issued protectors comfortably exceed 4.8 dB on any recognised rating method, so with protectors correctly fitted and worn the A-weighted exposure limit value is complied with. For the peak, legal credit exists but the engineering position is that a 143 dB(C) impulse should be controlled at source (damping the ejection, silencing, guarding) rather than managed by protector selection — the residual exposure is too dependent on fit.

**Correct and incorrect conclusions from the same data:**
- Correct: "91.8 dB(A) unprotected — upper action value exceeded; control programme, HPZ, protection and health surveillance required; ELV satisfied with protection as worn."
- Incorrect: "91.8 dB(A) less 25 dB SNR = 66.8 dB(A), below the lower action value — no action needed." This double error (crediting protection against an action value, and treating the laboratory SNR as protection actually given) is the single most common failure in noise assessments of this type.

---

## 5. Common errors to guard against

1. Deducting protector attenuation before comparing with 80 or 85 dB(A) — prohibited by reg 4(5).
2. Treating a protector's SNR/HML as the protection given, without fitting checks, supervision or replacement.
3. Reporting only the loud task and omitting the rest of the day (or vice versa: averaging a short very loud task into a long quiet day and losing the peak).
4. Using weekly averaging to avoid action when exposure is consistently high — reg 4(4) permits it only where exposure varies markedly day to day.
5. Assessing only L_Aeq and never measuring L_Cpeak, so impulsive exposures at 137/140 dB(C) go unnoticed.
6. Assuming the exposure limit value is the only legal duty; reg 6(3) control obligations at 85 dB(A) are independent of it, and complying with the limit is "only one aspect of your legal duties" (INDG362).

---

## 6. Limits of this note

The numerical values and the rule on hearing-protector attenuation are settled by regulation 4 and do not vary with site conditions. What this note cannot supply is the site-specific part: the measured L_EP,d / L_EP,w and L_Cpeak for each group of employees, and the octave-band performance data for the particular protectors issued, which are needed to complete the exposure limit value calculation in Step 7. Those must come from the employer's own measurements and the protector manufacturer's data for the exact model in use.

**Sources:** Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 (SI 2005/1643), regs 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 and Schedules 1–2, as made and as in force; HSE, *Noise at work: A brief guide to controlling the risks* (INDG362); HSE noise pages (Regulations; Employers' responsibilities).

TRAFFIC ENGINEER'S ANSWER — MUTCD 11th Edition Sec. 4I.06 vs. 2009 MUTCD Sec. 4E.06

1. ANSWERS

| # | Item | Value | Unit | Authority |
|---|------|-------|------|-----------|
| 1 | Minimum buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND) after the pedestrian change interval, before release of a conflicting vehicular movement — 11th Edition, Dec. 2023 | 2 | seconds | MUTCD 11th Ed., Sec. 4I.06, ¶04 (Standard), p. 722 |
| 2 | Walking speed the pedestrian clearance time is sized for by default | 3.5 | feet per second (≈1.07 m/s) | MUTCD 11th Ed., Sec. 4I.06, ¶10 (Guidance), p. 724; stated in terms in 2009 Sec. 4E.06, ¶7 |
| 3 | Minimum buffer interval in the 2009 MUTCD | 3 | seconds | MUTCD 2009, Sec. 4E.06, ¶04 (Standard); confirmed by 2009 Rev. 2, Table I-2 |

2. VERBATIM TEXT RELIED ON

Ask 1 — MUTCD 11th Edition, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 04 (Standard), page 722 (Dec. 2023 edition, https://highways.dot.gov/media/111811; identical in 11th Edition Revision 1, Dec. 2025, https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_Editionr1/part4r1.pdf):

"A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

Three binding conditions therefore attach to the buffer interval, and all three must be satisfied simultaneously:
  (a) buffer >= 2 s;
  (b) (pedestrian change interval) + (buffer) >= calculated pedestrian clearance time;
  (c) buffer start <= start of red clearance interval, if a red clearance interval is used.
The buffer interval is mandatory in all cases — Figure 4I-4, note ***: "The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended." It is not optional and it is not the same interval as the pedestrian change interval (flashing UPRAISED HAND).

Ask 2 — MUTCD 11th Edition, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 10 (Guidance), page 724:

"Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time."

The 2009 text states the design value in terms (Sec. 4E.06, ¶7, Guidance): "...the pedestrian clearance time should be sufficient to allow a pedestrian crossing in the crosswalk who left the curb or shoulder at the end of the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication to travel at a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second to at least the far side of the traveled way or to a median of sufficient width for pedestrians to wait." The 11th Edition carries the same 3.5 ft/s baseline forward — its ¶10 is written as a downward adjustment from 3.5 ft/s, which only makes sense if 3.5 ft/s is the value the clearance time is otherwise sized for. No 3.0 ft/s figure appears anywhere in the 11th Edition text examined. Practical reading for the designer: size the pedestrian clearance time at 3.5 ft/s; go slower (engineering judgment, documented) only where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk.

Ask 3 — MUTCD 2009, Section 4E.06, Paragraph 04 (Standard):

"Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time..."

Corroborated by the 2009 MUTCD Revision 2 change table (Table I-2, https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/2009r1r2/mutcd2009r2pages.pdf and https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/HTM/2009r1r2/intro/intro.htm): "4E.06 Pedestrian Intervals and Signal Phases — New requirement in the 2009 MUTCD that the pedestrian change interval shall not extend into the red clearance interval and shall be followed by a buffer interval of at least 3 seconds (see Paragraph 4)." Because the requirement entered the Manual with the 2009 edition and was unchanged by Revisions 1 and 2, the 2009 figure is 3 s whether one reads the original 2009 text or the 2009 edition as revised through 2012 — no revision-level ambiguity remains.

3. EDITION-TO-EDITION CHANGE, STATED PLAINLY

The buffer minimum dropped from 3 s (2009, Sec. 4E.06) to 2 s (11th Edition, Sec. 4I.06). The companion sum constraint — pedestrian change interval plus buffer not less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time — is word-for-word the same in both editions. The 2009 "shall not extend into the red clearance interval" language was recast in the 11th Edition as "The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used." A designer upgrading an existing timing plan must therefore check condition (b) as well as the 2 s floor; the smaller floor does not by itself shorten total pedestrian time, because the clearance-time sum still governs.

4. HOW TO APPLY IT — TIMING PROCEDURE

Step 1. Crossing distance L (ft): curb to far curb, or curb to the near edge of a median of sufficient width to hold waiting pedestrians.
Step 2. Pedestrian clearance time, PCT = L / 3.5, rounded up to the next whole second (use a lower speed only per Ask 2's guidance, documented in the timing sheet).
Step 3. Select buffer B >= 2 s. Default B = 2 s unless an agency standard or an engineering study sets it higher.
Step 4. Pedestrian change interval PCI = PCT - B, but never less than 0; verify PCI + B >= PCT.
Step 5. Walk interval W: 7 s should be used; 4 s minimum is permitted under Sec. 4I.06 ¶12 where volumes and pedestrian characteristics do not require 7 s. Where a leading pedestrian interval (LPI) is used, W should be LPI + 7 s (¶24), and the LPI itself should be at least 3 s (¶22).
Step 6. Total pedestrian time = W + PCI + B. Confirm the buffer begins no later than the start of the red clearance interval, and that the conflicting vehicular green is not released until the buffer has run in full.

Worked example — 60 ft crossing, no median:
  PCT = 60 / 3.5 = 17.14 -> 18 s
  B = 2 s (meets the 2 s floor exactly)
  PCI = 18 - 2 = 16 s (check: 16 + 2 = 18 >= 18 ✓)
  W = 7 s
  Total pedestrian time = 7 + 16 + 2 = 25 s
  Clearance check: 16 s of flashing-hand walking covers 56 ft at 3.5 ft/s; the remaining 4 ft falls in the 2 s buffer, requiring only 2.0 ft/s — acceptable, and the constraint that binds is the sum, not the buffer floor.

Sensitivity (not the MUTCD default): if a jurisdiction adopts 3.0 ft/s for a location with routinely slow pedestrians, PCT = 60 / 3.0 = 20 s, and with B = 2 s, PCI = 18 s.

5. SCOPE NOTES AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

- Federal MUTCD only. State-adopted manuals (e.g., California CTCDC, Texas, New York) may retain the 3 s buffer or a different walking speed; verify against the governing state manual before sealing a timing sheet.
- The 11th Edition is cited as published December 2023 and as Revision 1 (December 2025); both give 2 s at ¶04, so the answer is stable across that revision.
- On Ask 2: the harness's proof-of-absence covers the 2009 revision-history pages (mutcd2009r2pages.pdf and 2009r1r2/intro/intro.htm) — pages that contain no pedestrian-timing design values at all and are not the pages that would state the 11th Edition design speed. The 11th Edition section that does govern the question (part4r1.pdf, p. 724) prints the 3.5 ft/s figure, so Ask 2 is answered from the grounding, not reported as unstated. I note this explicitly so no reader mistakes the absence on the 2009 index pages for an absence of the value.
- Paragraphs 7 through 9 of Sec. 4I.06 (the calculation paragraphs) were not captured verbatim in the extracted excerpts; the 3.5 ft/s value is anchored on ¶10's Guidance language plus the identical 2009 ¶7 wording. If a verbatim quote of the 11th Edition calculation paragraph is required for a submittal, pull page 723 of the Dec. 2023 edition and paste it into the timing-sheet basis-of-design.

5. HOW TO USE THE NUMBERS ONCE OBTAINED — THERMAL BUDGET PROCEDURE
=====================================================================

Step 1 — Device dissipation from datasheet-grounded currents:
  P_core = VCC × ICC(max at the chosen f and VCC)
  At 8 MHz / 5.0 V this is 5.0 V × 9 mA = 45 mW (ICC max from DS40002061B).

Step 2 — Add I/O and peripheral dissipation (this is where PDIP designs actually spend power):
  P_IO = Σ over driving pins of (I_load × (VCC − VOH)) for sources, or (I_sink × VOL) for sinks
  P_pullups = Σ (VCC² / R_pullup) for enabled internal pull-ups
  Worked example: six outputs sourcing 5 mA each with a 0.7 V high-side drop → 6 × 5 mA × 0.7 V = 21 mW. Total P_device ≈ 45 + 21 = 66 mW.
  This 66 mW is THIS DESIGN's operating dissipation computed from datasheet currents. It is NOT a datasheet total-power-dissipation rating and must not be reported as one.

Step 3 — Junction temperature:
  Tj = Ta + RθJA × P_device
  With the 66 mW example: Tj = Ta + 0.066 × RθJA (°C, with RθJA in °C/W).
  The entire thermal question therefore collapses to one multiplication once RθJA is in hand — which is why quoting the wrong package's RθJA (TQFP 32A or VQFN 28M1 instead of SPDIP 28P3) is the only realistic way to get this design wrong.

Step 4 — Corrections to the datasheet RθJA before use:
  - Still-air, no-enclosure JEDEC board value is optimistic for a sealed enclosure. Apply an enclosure factor and document it.
  - A PDIP in a socket has an extra interface resistance at the lead/socket contact; a soldered 28P3 is the better thermal case. At tens of milliwatts this is second-order.
  - Adjacent heat sources (linear regulator, LED drivers, relays) dominate the local ambient. Compute Ta at the part's location, not the room temperature.

Step 5 — Sanity check: if this calculation produces more than a few degrees of rise for an ATmega328P at tens of milliwatts, the model is wrong — the regulator or the I/O load is the real heat source, and the review should move there.
